newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts give cautious welcome to Swedish budget.
newsitem.headline: Analysts give cautious welcome to Swedish budget.

text.p: Sweden's 1997 budget, presented to parliament on Friday, contained few surprises and was given a cautious welcome by analysts.
"You can see from the figures that the state finances have improved -- they've kept the promises they made," Aragon Securities analyst Tomas Niemela told Reuters.

With most of the measures in Finance Minister Erik Asbrink's first full budget already known to economists, there was little room for surprises and the fact that Asbrink announced no new budget savings next year left financial markets unruffled.
Comments in the budget on the development of Sweden's towering state debt were seen as a good sign.
"The positive thing is that they now have a target of achieving a budget surplus in 1999," Peter Lindqvist of HSBC Midland said.
The government said it would achieve balance in the state budget by 1998, and that it hoped to achieve a "permanent surplus" thereafter.
But the Social Democratic government's target of halving unemployment to four percent by the year 2000 was becoming more and more unrealistic, analysts said.
"Even if we have economic growth of three percent, I think it will be difficult to halve unemployment," Niemela said.
Growth in GDP is forecast at just 1.6 percent this year, rising to 2.3 percent in 1997.
A statement by Asbrink that he was prepared to take further measures to halve unemployment was interpreted as giving the issue lower priority.
"Since they see an opportunity to take further action next year, I don't think they really believe in halving unemployment themselves," Lindqvist said.
Even so, analysts welcomed the honesty with which the government increased its unemployment forecasts.
"It's quite reasonable that the outcome should be this way, it means the market has more confidence in the government," Swedbank economist Peter Granqvist said.
Thomas Lindberg, economist at Ohman stockbrokers, said the main thrust of the budget was not on the unemployment at all.
"The primary focus is to get Swedes more willing to spend money," he said.
Analysts said neither the Riksbank nor the government had given the market new signals on Swedish membership in the EU's exchange rate mechanism or the single currency.
"Speculation about Finnish membership has put the pressure on. That means that Sweden has found itself in the firing line and has to take a stance on the EMU and ERM," Granqvist said.
Analysts did not expect the Swedish crown to be pegged in the ERM before 1997.
"I should imagine that it might be on the agenda after the parliament's decision on EMU in 1997," Niemela said, adding that this was what the Riksbank had itself indicated.
